subject: Constraints on ODE Solver and gradient of posterior

messages.author: 7d0849fb70633078
messages.subject: Constraints on ODE Solver and gradient of posterior
parts:
I'm using the stiff ODE solver in command stan to try to fit 10 parameters in a 4 ODE system. Unfortunately I don't have data for three of the equations, but I do know that they two of them should be strictly decreasing functions and the third should be a strictly increasing function with all three functions becoming constant towards the end.

I guess one way to do this would be to have Stan reject any proposal where these functions don't meet those monotoniciity constraints, but I'm not sure how to do that. Alternatively, I know that for constrained parameters you guys sample on a transformed scale so you don't have to deal with a lot of rejections when you're in the wrong place of the posterior. I wonder if there is anything analogous to this I can do with my ODEs so that I'm sampling on a space where not meeting my monotonicity constraints is not even an option. The same way how you can sample rate parameters on a space where negative rate parameters aren't even an option.

The other thing I was wondering is how Stan computes the gradient of the posterior for ODEs. If I have the value of a function at 10 times points then to get the gradient of the log posterior I need the gradient of the solution with respect to the parameters. The solution however is being found by some complicated numerical technique. So how is Stan finding its gradient let alone finding it efficiently?

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Constraints on ODE Solver and gradient of posterior
parts:
> On Mar 30, 2016, at 5:36 PM, Arya Pourzanjani <ar...@umail.ucsb.edu> wrote:
>
> I'm using the stiff ODE solver in command stan to try to fit 10 parameters in a 4 ODE system. Unfortunately I don't have data for three of the equations, but I do know that they two of them should be strictly decreasing functions and the third should be a strictly increasing function with all three functions becoming constant towards the end.


> I guess one way to do this would be to have Stan reject any proposal where these functions don't meet those monotoniciity constraints,

How do you know if the functions aren't monotonic?
Is that monotonicity the function of parameters that
can be constrained to make the system monotonic?

> but I'm not sure how to do that. Alternatively, I know that for constrained parameters you guys sample on a transformed scale so you don't have to deal with a lot of rejections when you're in the wrong place of the posterior.

This is pretty critical for the algorithms; if you just
reject over boundaries, you can degrade to random walk behavior.

> I wonder if there is anything analogous to this I can do with my ODEs so that I'm sampling on a space where not meeting my monotonicity constraints is not even an option. The same way how you can sample rate parameters on a space where negative rate parameters aren't even an option.

> The other thing I was wondering is how Stan computes the gradient of the posterior for ODEs.
> If I have the value of a function at 10 times points then to get the gradient of the log posterior I need the gradient of the solution with respect to the parameters. The solution however is being found by some complicated numerical technique. So how is Stan finding its gradient let alone finding it efficiently?

If the solutions are y[1], ..., y[T], we're computing the
sensitivities, i.e., the gradient of each component of the solution
with respect to the parameters. We do it by creating a coupled
system of the state and the sensitivities using nested automtic
differentiation, then solve the coupled system using the numerical
integrator. The integrators for ODEs all work by stepwise simulation
of the system from the initial state to the solutions.

We wrote that up as part of our autodiff paper:

http://arxiv.org/abs/1509.07164

- Bob

messages.author: 97d82fedb7016adb
messages.subject: Re: Constraints on ODE Solver and gradient of posterior
parts:
Hi!

The most efficiet way to enforce your monotonicity is to constrain the parameters accordingly. The other (less efficient) way is to check in the ODE rhs function that the dy_dt's are always positive or negative. Whenever these conditions are not met, you fire a reject statement. This way the the ODE integration is aborted immediatley. So something like

  real dy_dt[3];

  ... calc dy_dt ...

  if(dy_dt[1] > 0 || dy_dt[2] > 0 || dy_dt[3] < 0)
    reject("Monotonicity is wrong!");

  return(dy_dt);

However, as I said, this is by far not as efficient as to constrain the paramters directly.

Best,
Sebastian
